meta.title: Greek Alphabet
meta.subtitle: 40 letters, letter pairs and signs in both directions · 10 reading rules
meta.desc: The Greek alphabet as Modern Greek uses it, and how it is read: 50 notes. The twenty-four letters in order, capital and small, each with its English and its Greek name; the 14 two-letter spellings, because Greek writes several single sounds with two letters (ου is [u], μπ is [b], ντ is [d]); the two signs, the accent and the diaeresis; and 10 reading rules. The first deck of the Greek collection. A letter, a pair or a sign is studied in both directions — see it and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall the letter — each a card with its own schedule; a reading rule is one card, a question and its answer. Every note gives the romanisation the level decks use, the sound, and one word that shows it with a speaker beside it: a word of Greek A1 wherever A1 has one, with the romanisation, the pronunciation and the meaning its A1 card gives (A1 has no word with γκ, τζ, υι or a diaeresis; those four examples are other dictionary words). THE ROMANISATION FOLLOWS THE SPELLING, NOT THE SOUND: it writes αι as ai, ει as ei, οι as oi, υ as y, ντ as nt and γκ as gk, so the sound is given beside it in the International Phonetic Alphabet, between square brackets, with an English word to compare. Greek spelling is regular to READ — a reader who knows these letters, pairs and rules can say any word aloud — and not to WRITE: the sound [i] is spelled six ways (η, ι, υ, ει, οι, υι) and [e] and [o] two ways each, so the sound side of those letters names the letter, and which spelling a word takes is learnt with the word. WHERE EVERY SOUND COMES FROM: each sound and English comparison is a cell of Wikipedia's pronunciation key for Greek (Help:IPA/Greek, revision 1373072501), each letter's names are those of the Letters table of Wikipedia's article "Greek alphabet" (revision 1387421171), and each rule is a sentence quoted, between quotation marks, from one of those two pages or from "Modern Greek phonology" (revision 1383354610), "Greek diacritics" (revision 1378374654) or "Greek orthography" (revision 1372376819); the plain line above a quotation says the same thing in a beginner's words and nothing more. The comparisons are approximations, as the key itself says. The example words' romanisations, pronunciations and meanings are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0); Wikipedia's text is CC BY-SA 4.0. THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). WHAT GREEK A1 ASKS OF A READER, counted on its 529 headwords: 161 hold a two-letter spelling and cannot be read one letter at a time; 286 hold an [i], an [e] or an [o] written otherwise than ι, ε or ο, which no rule predicts; 491 carry the accent; 131 end in ς; 19 are written with a capital, the days and the months; and 243 of A1's example sentences end in the Greek question mark. THE PACE: Folio deals ten new cards a day to a language deck unless you change it in the deck's options. A letter, a pair or a sign is two cards and a reading rule is one, so these 50 notes are 90 cards, 9 days; Greek A1 then runs from day 10 to day 115.

fields.Name: άλφα
fields.Sound: a · [a] Australian English father
fields.Example: άνθρωποςánthropos/ˈan.θɾo.pos/a human; person; the species man

fields.Name: βήτα
fields.Sound: v · [v] vet

fields.Name: γάμμα
fields.Sound: g · [ɣ] Spanish amigo; before e and i sounds [ʝ] similar to yes

fields.Name: δέλτα
fields.Sound: d · [ð] the

fields.Name: έψιλον
fields.Sound: e · [e] bet · the letter epsilon

fields.Name: ζήτα
fields.Sound: z · [z] between zone and genre (retracted)

fields.Name: ήτα
fields.Sound: i · [i] like neat · the letter eta

fields.Name: θήτα
fields.Sound: th · thought

fields.Name: ιώτα
fields.Sound: i · [i] like neat · the letter iota

fields.Name: κάππα
fields.Sound: k · [k] scar; before e and i sounds [c] skew
fields.Example: καφέςkafés/kaˈfes/cup of coffee

fields.Name: λάμδα
fields.Sound: l · [l] look

fields.Name: μυ
fields.Sound: m · [m] mole

fields.Name: νυ
fields.Sound: n · [n] no

fields.Name: ξι
fields.Sound: x · [ks] between dixon and diction (retracted)
fields.Example: ξέρωxéro/ˈkse.ɾo/to know of, be familiar with

fields.Name: όμικρον
fields.Sound: o · [o] chore · the letter omicron

fields.Name: πι
fields.Sound: p · [p] spy

fields.Name: ρο
fields.Sound: r · [r] similar to American English autumn or Scottish rule

fields.Name: σίγμα
fields.Sound: s · [s] between sip and ship (retracted)

fields.Name: ταυ
fields.Sound: t · [t] stay

fields.Name: ύψιλον
fields.Sound: y · [i] like neat · the letter upsilon
fields.Example: υπάρχωypárcho/iˈpar.xo/to exist, be, live

fields.Name: φι
fields.Sound: f · [f] four

fields.Name: χι
fields.Sound: ch · [x] Scottish English loch, German Bach; before e and i sounds [ç] hue

fields.Name: ψι
fields.Sound: ps · [ps] between opson and option (retracted)

fields.Name: ωμέγα
fields.Sound: o · [o] chore · the letter omega

fields.Ask: One letter, two small shapes. Which stands where?
fields.Rule: ς at the end of a word, σ everywhere else. The capital, Σ, has one shape.
fields.Quote: with ⟨ς⟩ being used in word-final position and ⟨σ⟩ elsewhere

fields.Name: ου
fields.Sound: ou · [u] pool (short)
fields.Example: δουλειάdouleiá/ðuˈʎa/employment, work, job

fields.Name: αι
fields.Sound: ai · [e] bet · two letters, the sound of ε

fields.Name: ει
fields.Sound: ei · [i] like neat · two letters, the sound of ι

fields.Name: οι
fields.Sound: oi · [i] like neat · two letters, the sound of ι

fields.Name: υι
fields.Sound: yi · [i] like neat · two letters, the sound of ι

fields.Name: αυ
fields.Sound: av · af · [av], or [af]: the υ is [v] vet, or [f] four “In Modern Greek, ⟨υ⟩, in ⟨αυ ευ ηυ⟩, is pronounced as [f] before a voiceless consonant or at the end of the word and [v] otherwise.”

fields.Name: ευ
fields.Sound: ev · ef · [ev], or [ef]: the υ is [v] vet, or [f] four “In Modern Greek, ⟨υ⟩, in ⟨αυ ευ ηυ⟩, is pronounced as [f] before a voiceless consonant or at the end of the word and [v] otherwise.”
fields.Example: ευχαριστώefcharistó/ef.xa.ɾiˈsto/thank you!, thanks!

fields.Name: μπ
fields.Sound: b · mp · [b] about, or [mb] inside a word “In Modern Greek, ⟨μπ, ντ, γκ, γγ⟩ are pronounced as prenasalised voiced stops [mb, nd, ɲɟ, ŋɡ] or voiced stops without nasalisation [b, d, ɟ, ɡ].”

fields.Name: ντ
fields.Sound: nt · [d] today, or [nd] inside a word “In Modern Greek, ⟨μπ, ντ, γκ, γγ⟩ are pronounced as prenasalised voiced stops [mb, nd, ɲɟ, ŋɡ] or voiced stops without nasalisation [b, d, ɟ, ɡ].” “Word-initially and after /r/ or /l/, they are very rarely, if ever, prenasalised.”

fields.Name: γκ
fields.Sound: gk · [ɡ] again; before e and i sounds [ɟ] argue “⟨γκ⟩ is also used to stand for [g] before vowels [a], [o] and [u], and [ɟ] before [e] and [i]”

fields.Name: γγ
fields.Sound: ng · [ŋɡ]: [ŋ] sing and [ɡ] again “⟨γγ⟩ and ⟨γκ⟩ are pronounced like English ⟨ng⟩ like in the word finger (not like in the word thing)”

fields.Name: γχ
fields.Sound: nch · the γ is [ŋ] sing, then χ “the letter ⟨γ⟩, before another velar consonant, stands for the velar nasal [ŋ]”
fields.Example: συγχωρώsynchoró/siŋ.xoˈɾo/to forgive, pardon, excuse

fields.Name: τσ
fields.Sound: ts · [t͡s] between cats and catch (retracted)

fields.Name: τζ
fields.Sound: tz · [d͡z] between buds and budge (retracted)
fields.Example: τζάμιtzámi/ˈd͡za.mi/window glass, glazing

fields.Letter: ά έ ή ί ό ύ ώ
fields.Name: ά έ ή ί ό ύ ώ
fields.Sound: the accent, in Greek the tonos: it marks the stressed syllable “It uses only a single accent mark, the acute (also known in this context as tonos, i.e. simply 'accent'), marking the stressed syllable of polysyllabic words, and occasionally the diaeresis to distinguish diphthongal from digraph readings in pairs of vowel letters”
fields.Example: ποτέpoté/poˈte/ever; at any time

fields.Name: ϊ ϋ
fields.Sound: the diaeresis, two dots over the second of two vowel letters: the two are read one after the other, not as a pair (o-i, where οι is [i]); an accent on the FIRST of the two letters does the same (άι) “It uses only a single accent mark, the acute (also known in this context as tonos, i.e. simply 'accent'), marking the stressed syllable of polysyllabic words, and occasionally the diaeresis to distinguish diphthongal from digraph readings in pairs of vowel letters” “Also ⟨άι⟩ and sometimes ⟨άϊ⟩.”
fields.Example: κοροϊδεύωkoroïdévo/ko.ɾoi̯ˈðe.vo/to mock, ridicule, tease, make fun of

fields.Ask: The same word three ways. Where has the accent gone?
fields.Rule: On a capital letter the accent stands to its left; a word written all in capitals has none.
fields.Quote: In uppercase (all-caps), accents and breathings are eliminated, in titlecase they appear to the left of the letter rather than above it.

fields.Ask: What is the mark at the end?
fields.Rule: A question mark. Greek writes ; where English writes ?
fields.Quote: The principal difference is the Greek question mark ⟨;⟩

fields.Show: η ι υ ει οι υι
fields.Rule: One: every one of them is [i]. Reading is safe; which of the six a word is written with is learnt with the word.
fields.Quote: In Modern Greek, ⟨η, ῃ, ει, ι, οι, υ, υι⟩ all represent [i]

fields.Ask: Two pairs of spellings. How many sounds?
fields.Rule: Two: ε and αι are both [e], ο and ω are both [o].
fields.Quote: In Modern Greek, ⟨ε, αι⟩ represent [e], and ⟨ο, ω⟩ represent [o].
fields.Example: ωραίοςoraíos/oˈɾe.os/good, fine, nice

fields.Ask: γ, κ and χ change before two sounds. Which, and how?
fields.Show: γε γι · κε κι · χε χι
fields.Rule: Before an e or an i sound they are made further forward in the mouth: γ like the y of yes, κ like the k of skew, χ like the h of hue.
fields.Quote: In Modern Greek, ⟨κ; γκ, γγ; γ; χ⟩ are pronounced as palatal [c, ɟ, ʝ, ç] before the front vowels [e i], and velar [k, ɡ, ɣ, x] in other cases.

fields.Rule: Two. Here the ι before a vowel is not a syllable of its own: it only changes the consonant before it.
fields.Quote: The velars also merge with a following nonsyllabic /i/ to the corresponding palatal before the vowels /a, o, u/, e.g. χιόνι [ˈçoni]

fields.Ask: Two of the same consonant. Is it said twice, or longer?
fields.Rule: No: a doubled consonant is said as one.
fields.Quote: Modern Standard Greek does not have geminate consonants

fields.Ask: How is the σ said here?
fields.Rule: As [z]: σ before a voiced consonant is voiced.
fields.Quote: ⟨σ⟩ is pronounced as voiced [z] before a voiced consonant.

fields.Ask: Does a word keep its stress in every form?
fields.Rule: No. The stress falls on one of the last three syllables and can stand on a different one in another form of the same word, so the accent is read on every form.
fields.Quote: Modern Greek has variable (phonologically unpredictable) stress. Every multisyllabic word carries stress on one of its three final syllables. … The position of the stress can vary between different inflectional forms of the same word within its inflectional paradigm.
fields.Example: άνθρωποςánthropos/ˈan.θɾo.pos/a human; person; the species man
